title: Germany news: Leftist BSW rules out limiting ties with far-right AfD
summary: A motion had been filed by senior BSW leaders to reject any "de facto" support of a far-right government. Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht has said limited cooperation could provide a "window of…

image.caption: 'We are ready to talk:' The BSW federal party congress met in Dresden on SatrudayImage: Jens Schlüter/AFP

blocks.text: Left-wing BSW party votes against measure limiting cooperation with far-right AfD

blocks.caption: BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht rejected a formal partnership with the far right, but says there is limited scope for cooperation Image: Jens Schlüter/AFP

blocks.text: The left-wing populist party Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (also BSW) voted against a measure that would have limited cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) on the federal level.

During the party conference in the eastern city of Dresden, a majority of the approximately 600 delegates voted against a motion put forth by several founding BSW members calling for a clearer distinction from the far right.

The basis for the vote came after the AfD came out on top in September's state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with 39 seats. The victory is being seen as a major win for Germany's far right. In October, the AfD's Tobias Rausch in Saxony-Anhalt became Germany's first far-right state parliament speaker since World War II.
With the BSW's five seats, the two parties on the opposite extremes of the political spectrum would combine for a majority of the 83 seats.
BSW Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht and party leader Fabio De Masi have advocated for the-called "Magdeburg Model," named after the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.

This approach rejects a formal coalition with the AfD, offers no support for AfD candidate in the election of a state premiere, and calls for no official tolerance for far-fight platforms. However, the approach envisions joint motions, joint voting, and possibly also written agreements with the AfD.
AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt
Wagenknecht says AfD 'not a long term partner'
On Saturday, Wagenknecht made clear she does not see the AfD as a long-term strategic partner.

"None of us wants to cozy up to the AfD," Wagenknecht said. But the BSW will decide how to proceed if there is "the possibility of reasonable majorities for peace, social improvement, and a reform of public broadcasting."

The AfD and BSW see some overlap in Germany's approach to the Ukraine war, with both taking pro-Russia views critical of military support for Kyiv, while opposing or questioning sanctions on Russia, arguing that they harm the German economy.

BSW executive board members such as Christian Leye, Amid Rabieh and Klaus Ernst had sought to pass the amendment to both rule out coalitions with the AfD, and also "any formal or de facto tolerance, support for an AfD-led government, and long-term agreements on cooperation."
"Since when have we been partners with the AfD?" Leye said after the vote. "This party can only be an opponent."
"In my view, it is a racist party, a nationalist party that also has its issues with democracy. That is why it cannot be a partner," he said.
Germany's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, has classified the AfD as right-wing extremist.
